transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-27 14:00 UTC | Duration: 38m | Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Hawthorne Head of ML), Jonas Reed (VP Eng), Priya Singh (Security)

Summary: quick discovery to understand reliability needs, current infra, desired SLOs, and compliance constraints. Request to validate multi-region fallbacks and how Redwood handles incident tolerance across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.

[00:00] Sophie: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm sophie from redwood, i'm the AE on this account, with liam our solutions eng.
[00:08] Liam: hey all, quick heads up i'll be digging into the technical routing and failover bits — happy to answer infra questions.
[00:15] Maya: thanks; quick context — we run a payments fraud scoring API, p95 p99 are huge for us, we need near-zero tail spikes during peak. evaluating hosted vs dedicated; also we may need private for data residency.
[00:32] Jonas: timeline: pilot in april if benchmarks look good, procurement in may.
[00:38] Priya: from security, SOC2 mandatory, KMS/HSM for keys, audit logs retention 1 year, and SSO (SAML) is needed.
[00:47] Sophie: great, that's helpful. liam, can you run through how redwood approaches region failover and fallbacks?
[00:55] Liam: sure. high level — requests route by policy, we do primary-region affinity, but we have automatic fallback to secondary region or to model variants if primary capacity is out. there are a few knobs: cross-region sync of KV cache, we can do prefix caching and route reads to cached nodes to reduce cold kv misses.
[01:15] Maya: quick q — how do you keep cache warm across regions? cross-region replication?
[01:20] Liam: yeah it's an async replication for KV cache; it's eventual but tuned for high hit-rates; for strict SLOs customers sometimes prefer active-active with sticky routing or dedicated capacity per region. active-active reduces failover latency but costs more.
[01:34] Jonas: how fast is failover? seconds? minutes?
[01:37] Liam: depends — for routing failover we can route within a second to a healthy region if the control plane sees node errors. KV warming may take longer — tens of seconds for cold paths. for most completion workloads we keep a small prefix cache warm to avoid big tail spikes.
[01:52] Maya: that matters — our p99 budget is 300ms for inference. do you have customers meeting that on hosted?
[01:58] Liam: yes some customers do on hosted with optimized models and small seq lengths; but cost and region proximity matter. for strict p99 300ms we usually see dedicated capacity or private with pinned GPUs gives the most predictable tail.
[02:12] Priya: what about SLA? do you offer a latency SLA?
[02:16] Sophie: we offer uptime SLAs on Dedicated; latency SLOs are provided as guidance and performance profiles. for Hosted we publish performance profiles but not hard latency SLAs; Dedicated can come with SLA addendum for uptime and latency tiers in enterprise contracts.
[02:31] Jonas: can you explain fallback to model variants? so if main model is overloaded you drop to smaller model?
[02:36] Liam: exactly — policy-based fallback: same family smaller quantized artifact, or a faster model that approximates output. we call it model-variant fallback; it preserves functional continuity but may have slight quality regressions. customers define acceptable regressions.
[02:48] Maya: do you support multi-region active-active for KV coherence?
[02:52] Liam: we do active-active for certain Dedicated/private deployments; it requires extra setup and networking, and for private we can integrate with your VPC peering. tradeoff is complexity and higher egress/sync costs.
[03:06] Priya: on compliance — audit logs, do you provide immutable logs and retention controls?
[03:11] Sophie: yes, we surface audit logs in the console; for Private/Dedicated we can offer extended retention and forward to your SIEM. we support customer-managed KMS in Private and Dedicated for key wrapping.
[03:24] Jonas: network-wise, if we go Private on-prem we need air-gap option for compliance — do you have an on-prem package?
[03:30] Liam: yes we have a private on-prem distribution; it includes the control plane option with offline attestations; typical enterprise deal for that has a longer onboarding window.
[03:39] Maya: some nitty-gritty: during failover, are requests dropped or queued? we absolutely can't drop transactions.
[03:45] Liam: we design for graceful degradation: if primary region becomes unhealthy, traffic will route to fallback regions; if a model is not available we'll route to variant. we don't queue at the gateway for long durations — we rely on routing + retries. if total capacity is exhausted, requesters receive 5xx — we recommend circuit-breaker on client side and client-side retries with backoff.
[04:03] Jonas: what observability do we get for these events?
[04:06] Sophie: console has per-route dashboards, token-level latency histograms, error traces, and events for failover. we can also ship alerts to pager duty.
[04:14] Priya: do you have runbooks for incident scenarios we can review?
[04:18] Liam: yes we'll include runbooks in the security pack and a sample incident timeline; plus guidance for client retry/backoff settings.
[04:26] Maya: about pricing — what's the cost delta between hosted and dedicated for predictable tail latency?
[04:31] Sophie: dedicated has a reserved capacity pricing + lower per-token cost at scale; hosted is pay-as-you-go but can see more variance. we'll share a tailored pricing sheet after we get your traffic profile.
[04:41] Maya: we can share a 7-day traffic snapshot with seq length distribution and tps.
[04:45] Sophie: perfect, that will help liam set realistic benchmark config.
[04:49] Jonas: on multi-region failover, are there cross-region data residency issues? if we route to eu from us during failover that's a problem.
[04:57] Liam: we support region pinning and routing policies that respect data residency; you can configure allowed failover regions per dataset or tenant. for strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private where we can enforce region-only routing.
[05:11] Priya: encryption: at rest and in transit? and KMS key control?
[05:15] Sophie: in transit TLS, at rest encryption by default; customer-managed KMS for Private/Dedicated so you hold wrapping keys.
[05:22] Maya: do you do chaos test drills / runbook rehearsals with customers?
[05:26] Liam: we support joint chaos testing during pilot — we can simulate region outages and measure failover times. we recommend a staged approach: smoke, canary, full failover.
[05:36] Maya: that'd be great. we'll want times to be under 2s for routing and p99 within 300ms after failover, is that realistic?
[05:44] Liam: 2s route switch is realistic for routing; p99 300ms after failover is tougher unless you have warmed caches or active-active; we can aim for that in Dedicated active-active with warmed caches and pinned GPUs.
[05:58] Jonas: procurement question — if we pick Dedicated can we start with Hosted for pilot then migrate with same API?
[06:04] Sophie: yes, same API and SDKs across modes. migration path is part of our onboarding playbook.
[06:10] Maya: can liam outline the benchmark you'll run? what inputs do you need?
[06:15] Liam: need a traffic snapshot, seq length distribution, model choice, and target SLOs. we'll run steady-state throughput and failover simulation with region kill and measure p95/p99 and cold-cache tail.
[06:28] Maya: we'll send that data.
[06:30] Sophie: ok next steps recap — i'll send security pack + SOC2, liam will share benchmark plan and pricing scenarios, maya and jonas will share traffic profile and confirm stakeholders. schedule follow-up 4/3.
[06:42] Priya: any competitors we should be aware of? we looked at bedrock and some self-host triton setups.
[06:48] Sophie: noted. we'll include comparison notes, but main differentiator is production-grade rollout and observability.
[06:55] Jonas: i think that's all, thanks.
[06:58] Sophie: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email.

End of transcript.
